implementation_notes: Scala 2.13's mutable buffer carries the operation directly: ArrayBuffer.trimToSize() 'Trims the ArrayBuffer to an appropriate size for the current number of elements (rounding up to the next natural size), which may replace the array by a shorter one' - note that the result is the implementation's natural size and not exactly size(). The same class provides the right-sizing companions sizeHint(size) to reserve before a bulk fill and clearAndShrink(size) to empty and shrink in one call, while its removal methods only move elements ('Note: This does not actually resize the internal representation. See trimToSize if you want to also resize internally'). Immutable collections (List, Vector, Seq) have no capacity to trim at all: their equivalent is to build the right-sized value from the survivors (take, filter, toVector) and drop the old one.
pitfalls: trimToSize() rounds up to the next natural size, so it bounds memory without promising capacity == size - the same 'non-binding' flavour as C++ shrink_to_fit.
The buffer must be quiesced: the call may replace the backing array, so an Array obtained through toArray before the trim (or a parallel writer on a shared buffer) is looking at the old storage.

Immutable collections cannot be trimmed at all: choosing Vector/List means the peak-shaped intermediate lives until the last reference to it disappears, so take/filter rebuilds are the only available trim.
